articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content_excerpt: No amount of rhetoric and threats of aggression will undermine its people’s will to protect its sovereignty and national integrity, Iran reiterated in the context of talks about the Donald Trump administration’s possible escalation in the war after being crushed in the US midterm elections. Though Trump admitted that the US-Israeli war on Iran was the main factor in his Republican Party’s losses in the November 3 midterm elections, he attempted to justify his decision to go to the war and even said he will do it again if necessary. articles.title: Follow the money: billionaire spending on the 2026 midterms
articles.author: Amanda Yee
articles.content_excerpt: OpenSecrets published its list of top donors to outside groups this election cycle, and the top ten is a “who’s who” of billionaires: Elon Musk, casino magnate Miriam Adelson, former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg, and tech oligarchs Benjamin Horowitz, Marc Andreessen, and Paul Singer all made the list. And although Republicans outraised and outspent Democrats across the board, the real story isn’t the party split. It’s who is writing the checks, and what they’re buying. In particular, three special interest groups spent historic amounts to capture Congress: AIPAC, Big Tech, and crypto. articles.title: Ireland to explore scenarios for constitutional future, including unity
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content_excerpt: Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin recently announced plans to establish a government body to prepare for different scenarios for the country’s constitutional future, including the possibility of a united Ireland. articles.title: The bees in the city: organizing China’s delivery workers in Ganzhou
articles.author: Tings Chak
articles.content_excerpt: At the entrance to Xingfuli, a residential compound in Ganzhou, Jiangxi province, a bulletin board displays the names, photographs, and phone numbers of the people responsible for managing the neighborhood. Though an ordinary bulletin board at first appearance, among the building representatives and Communist Party members is an unexpected name: Kang Jiafei, a food delivery worker who is also listed as a community “grid worker.” China has more than ten million food delivery workers, part of a rapidly growing global workforce whose lives are organized by algorithms, tight deadlines, and orders that take them across the city. They are among the most visible workers on China’s streets, yet often have no fixed workplace, no place to rest between orders, and limited access to conventional forms

articles.title: Trump-nominated WFP head has no credible plan to address fund crunch
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content_excerpt: “The number one thing we can do to reduce hunger in the world is to reduce the amount of conflict that is happening all around the world,” Luke Lindberg, the new executive director of the World Food Program (WFP), said in his first media address last week. Conflict is the main driver of hunger today, driving two-thirds of the acute food insecurity affecting 266 million people worldwide. “Conflict is a man-made situation. It is something that we can solve,” added Lindberg, who assumed office on October 26. Earlier this year, the WFP said that the “conflict in the Middle East” – a catch-all phrase for Israeli genocide in Gaza, US-Israeli war on Iran, and the Saudi war on Yemen – “is deepening this food crisis to an alarming degree,” warning of “record numbers of acute hunger if it continues.

articles.content_excerpt: Democrats just flipped Congress in a landslide, turned Texas blue, and won a Kansas Senate seat for the first time in nearly a century. Khalek lays out how midterm voters delivered a massive rebuke to Trump’s war on Iran, ICE terror, and soaring cost of living, electing insurgent progressives across the country.
